items.title: Q1 · June 2012 (Paper II)
items.meta: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary British/Irish & American Literature · Unit IX: Literary Theory Post-WWII · Jacques Derrida
items.stem:
To refer to the unresolvable difficulties
a text may open up, Derrida makes use
of the term

structured.lead:
To refer to the unresolvable difficulties
a text may open up, Derrida makes use of the term
structured.options_hint: aporia difference erasure supplement

items.explanation: Adopted from Greek philosophy (meaning an 'unpassable path'), aporia is used by Jacques Derrida in deconstruction to denote a point of undecidability or an unresolvable logical impasse where a text contradicts and undermines its own rhetorical premises.

structured.fallback:
Arrange the following in the chronological order :
1. Mary Wollstonecraft's Vindication of the Rights of Women
2. Lyrical Ballads
3. French Revolution
4. Percy's Reliques of Ancient English Poetry

items.explanation: The correct chronological sequence is Thomas Percy's Reliques of Ancient English Poetry (1765), the outbreak of the French Revolution (1789), Mary Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), and Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads (1798), giving 4, 3, 1, 2.

structured.lead: Which poem by Chaucer was written on the death of Blanche, Wife of John of Gaunt ?
structured.options_hint: Troilus and Criseyde The House of Fame T

items.explanation: Geoffrey Chaucer's first major poem, The Book of the Duchess (c. 1368–72), is an octosyllabic dream-vision elegy written to commemorate Blanche of Lancaster, the first wife of Chaucer's patron John of Gaunt, following her death in 1368.

items.explanation: Irish poet Seamus Heaney was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1995 'for works of lyrical beauty and ethical depth' (while Ted Hughes and Geoffrey Hill never won the Nobel Prize). items.explanation: In the opening line of W. H. Auden's poem 'September 1, 1939' (written upon the outbreak of World War II), the American colloquial noun 'dives' refers to a cheap, dimly lit bar or night club in Manhattan's 52nd Street jazz district.

Christopher Marlowe are true ?
I.
Edward II was written in the last year of Marlowe's life.
II.
Many critics consider Doctor
Faustus  to be Marlowe's best play.
III.
His Spanish Tragedy comes  a close second.
IV.
Marlowe was less educated than
Shakespeare
structured.options_hint: I and II are true II and III are true II

items.explanation: Statements I and II are true: Edward II (c. 1592–93) was written near the end of Christopher Marlowe's life, and Doctor Faustus is widely regarded as his finest play. Statement III is false because The Spanish Tragedy was written by Thomas Kyd, and Statement IV is false because Marlowe held a Master of Arts degree from Cambridge.

structured.lead: "Art for Art's Sake" became a rallying cry for
structured.options_hint: Aesthetes Symbolists Imagists Art Noveau

items.explanation: Translated from the French slogan l'art pour l'art, 'Art for Art's Sake' became the rallying cry of the late nineteenth-century Aesthetic Movement (the Aesthetes), championed in Britain by Walter Pater, Algernon Charles Swinburne, and Oscar Wilde.

structured.options_hint: The General Prologue' is appended to The

options: The General Prologue' is appended to The Canterbury Tales
In all, Chaucer tells thirty tales in this work
The Canterbury Tales remained unfinished at the time of its author's death
The Wife of Bath, The Clerk, Sir Gawain and The Franklin are characters and tale-tellers in this work
items.explanation: Geoffrey Chaucer's The Canterbury Tales remained unfinished at his death in 1400: although Harry Bailly's scheme in the General Prologue proposes 120 stories (four tales from each of roughly thirty pilgrims), Chaucer completed only 24 tales.

items.explanation: Coined by drama critic Irving Wardle in 1958, 'comedy of menace' describes the early plays of Harold Pinter—such as The Room (1957), The Birthday Party (1958), and The Dumb Waiter (1957)—in which ordinary comic dialogue is underscored by vague, looming terror and intimidation.

items.explanation: Ben Jonson's Volpone (1606) is a satirical Jacobean city comedy about greed and legacy-hunting, whereas Shakespeare's Hamlet, John Webster's The Duchess of Malfi, and Norton and Sackville's Gorboduc are all tragedies centred on blood revenge.

structured.options_hint: A word with roots in a native language A

options: A word with roots in a native language
A word whose meaning changes with every renewed use
A word newly coined or used in a new sense
An obsession with new words and phrases
items.explanation: A neologism (from Greek neos 'new' and logos 'word') is a newly coined word or expression, or an existing word used in a new sense.

structured.lead:
"You have seen how a man was made
a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man" is an example of
structured.options_hint: Bathos Epistrophe Chiasmus Anti-climax J

items.explanation: This famous sentence from Frederick Douglass's Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845) is a classic example of chiasmus (specifically antimetabole), a rhetorical device in which words or grammatical structures are repeated in inverted order (A-B : B-A).

In a poem, a line may either be end-
stopped or

structured.lead: In a poem, a line may either be endstopped or
structured.options_hint: rhymed broken accented run-on

items.explanation: In prosody, a line of verse is either end-stopped (when its syntactic unit and meaning pause naturally at the line's end) or a run-on line (marked by enjambment, where the sense and syntax carry over without pause into the next line).

is an example of

structured.lead: "The pen is mightier than the sword" is an example of
structured.options_hint: simile image conceit metonymy

items.explanation: Coined by Edward Bulwer-Lytton in his 1839 play Richelieu, 'The pen is mightier than the sword' is a classic example of metonymy, in which closely associated objects—'the pen' and 'the sword'—stand respectively for the written word and military force.

structured.lead: An epilogue is
structured.options_hint: prefixed to a text which it introduces.

options: prefixed to a text which it introduces.
suffixed to a text which it sums up or extends.
a piece of writing or speech that formally begins a book.
a piece of writing or speech that bears no relation to the text at hand.
items.explanation: An epilogue (the opposite of a prologue) is a concluding section or speech suffixed to the end of a literary work or play that sums up, comments on, or extends the action of the text.
